description:
This project was built to draw inspiration from the 2024 film "The Count of Monte Cristo," specifically the beautiful shots of the tartane approaching the island. I spent about four weeks on this during my free time. Please note that this is an artistic interpretation and not a perfectly historically or geographically accurate representation. It allowed me to experiment with fluid simulations; while my hardware limitations kept me from pushing the resolution to the extreme, it was a great opportunity to test various techniques, such as dynamic paint and pure shader setups, before settling on a dedicated fluid simulation.

Workflow
- Modeling and texturing in Blender 5.1. The tartane was created using plans found on Wikipedia and a basic mesh produced by fan3d on Sketchfab, which I refined, remodelled and completely retextured using custom procedural shaders (wood, nailed planks, fabric, rusty metal, rope). The island was generated in Gaea 2.2 and exported as 8K heightmaps, refined with procedural shaders in Blender. For vegetation, I modified, simplified, and retextured Quixel Aleppo Pines, scattering them across the island using custom mask data exported from Gaea. The ocean is a massive plane driven by procedural setups with adaptive subdivision and displacement. I also added a simple character on deck for scale.
- Simulations: The sails are driven by a basic Blender cloth simulation reacting to a wind force field modulated in strength and direction using noise. For the water, I opted for FLIP Fluids v1.8.6 (self-compiled from the GitHub repository) for the local domain around the hull (resolution 400, baked over 1h37 using 20 threads, 10,000,000 fluid particles, and up to 20,000 whitewater particles). To seamlessly merge the simulation into the ocean, I used a Lattice modifier to align both surfaces at the border, combined with a transparency mask in the ocean shader to keep negative fluid elevations visible.
- Lighting and atmosphere: Lit simply using the new Blender Sky Texture. I added a large bounding container with a low-density Principled Volume to create atmospheric depth.
- Animation relies on native keyframes, utilizing Noise Modifiers in the graph editor for the hull movement, and Camera Shakify for subtle camera dynamics.
- Rendering with Cycles OptiX (2.39:1, 3840x1608px, 1024 samples, ~5 minutes per frame). Frames were exported as Linear Rec.709 OpenEXR files. For the first time, I rendered everything directly via the command line (terminal), which prevented UI crashes on heavy frames. I used various focal lengths, such as 50mm, 40mm, and 20mm for drone-style perspectives.
- Compositing, color grading, final editing, and sound design with DaVinci Resolve Studio 21.

PC Configuration
- Ubuntu 26.04 LTS
- 16 GB DDR5
- Intel Core i7-12700H
- NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Laptop GPU

Software
- Blender 5.1
- Gaea 2.2
- FLIP Fluids 1.8
- DaVinci Resolve Studio 21
